passage: That the printing press caused the Reformation has the appeal of a tidy mechanism: cheap Bibles and pamphlets let Luther's ideas outrun the Church's power to suppress them. The claim is not so much false as incomplete. Printing had existed for over half a century before 1517 without fracturing Christendom; the same presses served the Church as readily as its critics, pouring out indulgences and orthodox devotionals in far greater volume than heretical tracts. What the press supplied was not a message but a capacity, neutral as to content. It amplified whatever entered it—reform and reaction alike. To credit the technology with the outcome is to overlook that a tool magnifies existing forces without choosing among them; the press made the Reformation faster and louder, not inevitable.
prompt: Which choice states an inference best supported by the passage?
choices: A technology can accelerate a movement without being the decisive cause of it.
The printing press had no meaningful effect on how quickly Reformation ideas spread.
The Church's own use of the press, which poured out indulgences, caused the Reformation.
Without the printing press, the Reformation could not have occurred at all.
correct_answer: A technology can accelerate a movement without being the decisive cause of it.

passage: Intuition casts memory as a recording: an event is filed away intact and, on recall, played back. Neuroscience has dismantled this picture. When a consolidated memory is retrieved, it becomes briefly labile—chemically vulnerable—and must be stabilized anew, a process called reconsolidation. During that window the memory can be altered, weakened, or updated before it is re-stored, so that each act of remembering can subtly rewrite what is remembered. The very neural mechanism that lets us update old knowledge with new experience also means a frequently recalled memory may drift furthest from the event it purports to preserve. This is not a design flaw but a feature: a memory system built to guide future action gains more from staying current than from staying faithful. Fidelity to the past, it turns out, was never memory's primary job—an unsettling conclusion for anyone who has trusted a vivid recollection as proof of what occurred.
prompt: According to the text, it can most reasonably be inferred that a memory recalled frequently
choices: is preserved most accurately, because repeated rehearsal strengthens it
becomes permanently fixed and immune to any further change
is stored in a different region of the brain than a rarely recalled one
may diverge more from the original event than one that is rarely recalled
correct_answer: may diverge more from the original event than one that is rarely recalled

passage: Nineteenth-century geology enshrined uniformitarianism: the present is the key to the past, and the slow processes we observe—erosion, sedimentation—suffice, given enough time, to explain the rock record. Catastrophism, with its floods and sudden upheavals, was dismissed as unscientific special pleading. Modern geology has quietly rehabilitated catastrophe, but on uniformitarian terms. The asteroid impact that closed the Cretaceous was sudden and violent, yet it invoked no forces alien to physics as we know it; rare, high-magnitude events are simply the tail of the same distribution that includes the daily and the gradual. The lesson is not that Lyell was wrong to insist on known causes, but that he wrongly equated 'known causes' with 'gentle and frequent ones.' Uniformity of law, it turns out, does not entail uniformity of rate.
prompt: Which choice is the most reasonable inference about the modern view described in the passage?
choices: The processes that shaped the Earth have always operated at a roughly constant rate, uniform in their magnitude as well as in their kind.
Catastrophism has now replaced uniformitarianism as the governing framework of geology, overturning Lyell's insistence on known causes.
A sudden, violent geological event can be consistent with the principle that only known physical causes shaped Earth's history.
Lyell was correct in holding that gradual processes acting over immense spans of time explain the entire rock record by themselves.
correct_answer: A sudden, violent geological event can be consistent with the principle that only known physical causes shaped Earth's history.

passage: The idea that bringing hostile groups into contact will erode their prejudices has an appealing simplicity, and decades of studies confirm that contact often does reduce bias. The finding is real; the simplicity is deceptive. Early researchers were explicit that contact helps only when certain conditions hold—when the groups meet as equals, pursue shared goals, and act with institutional support. Absent these, contact can as easily entrench hostility as dissolve it, as anyone who has watched rival factions share cramped quarters can attest. Later analyses complicate the picture further: some of the prejudice-reducing effect appears to spread to group members never actually encountered, while some evaporates once the structured setting is left behind. The evidence thus supports a claim narrower than the slogan—that contact of a particular, engineered kind reliably reduces prejudice—and warns against the broader inference that mere exposure will do the work on its own.

choices: Evidence that a program meeting the classic conditions—equal status, shared goals, institutional support—sharply reduced participants' bias

A study showing that contact under unequal, competitive conditions increased hostility between groups
correct_answer: A large study showing that people who merely lived alongside an out-group, with no shared goals or institutional support, developed durably lower prejudice

passage: Renaissance linear perspective is routinely described as the moment painting learned to tell the truth—a window onto the world, geometry in the service of the eye. The system does model one fact of vision: objects diminish with distance toward a single vanishing point. Yet that point is fixed for a single, motionless, monocular viewer, an eye that does not exist. Real seeing is binocular, mobile, and continuous; perspective freezes it into an abstraction and then presents the abstraction as nature. In doing so it quietly installs the viewer as the still center around which the visible world is ordered. Perspective's claim to objectivity is thus also its most artful fiction: it naturalizes a particular way of looking, and a particular looker, as looking itself.
prompt: Which choice is most strongly supported by the text?
choices: Linear perspective faithfully reproduces the way human eyes actually perceive the world.
Linear perspective presents a constructed viewpoint as if it were an unmediated record of vision.
Linear perspective fails to capture even the diminishment of objects with distance.
Renaissance painters adopted perspective chiefly to flatter the patrons who commissioned their work.
correct_answer: Linear perspective presents a constructed viewpoint as if it were an unmediated record of vision.

passage: A popular history casts the acceptance of continental drift as a simple triumph of evidence over stubborn dogma: Wegener was right, his critics were blinkered, and the fossils vindicated him. The truth is less flattering to hindsight. Wegener's contemporaries rejected his theory not out of mere prejudice but because he could specify no plausible mechanism—no force strong enough to plow continents through solid ocean floor—and the mechanism he did propose was demonstrably too weak. Their skepticism was, by the evidential standards of the day, reasonable. Drift was ultimately accepted only when seafloor spreading supplied the missing mechanism decades later. To celebrate Wegener as a lone visionary crushed by dogmatists is thus to misdescribe the episode: it was not that his critics ignored good reasoning, but that the reasoning available to everyone, Wegener included, was genuinely incomplete.
prompt: What is the main rhetorical purpose of the passage?
choices: To argue that Wegener's critics were driven by professional dogma, and that the popular history has if anything understated how much prejudice shaped their resistance.
To revise a heroic narrative by showing that the resistance to Wegener reflected a real evidential gap rather than closed-mindedness.
To demonstrate that the fossil evidence marshalled on Wegener's behalf was never strong enough to establish that the continents had once been joined.
To establish that Wegener himself anticipated seafloor spreading, and that the mechanism his critics kept demanding had in fact already been supplied.
correct_answer: To revise a heroic narrative by showing that the resistance to Wegener reflected a real evidential gap rather than closed-mindedness.

passage: It is tempting to narrate the triumph of equal temperament as the victory of mathematical rationality over messy acoustic reality. By dividing the octave into twelve identical semitones, the system let keyboard players modulate freely among all keys—a convenience earlier tunings denied. Yet the story is less a tale of progress than of loss deliberately chosen. Equal temperament makes every interval except the octave slightly out of tune; the pure thirds and fifths that earlier temperaments preserved in favored keys are sacrificed uniformly. Musicians did not adopt the system because it sounded better—by the older standard it sounded worse—but because it traded local purity for global flexibility. What its champions call rationalization, then, might as fairly be called an aesthetic compromise: a decision to distribute imperfection evenly rather than to concentrate it where it would least be heard. Progress here names not the removal of a flaw but its equitable redistribution.
prompt: The passage is primarily structured as
choices: a call to abandon equal temperament and restore the earlier temperaments whose thirds and fifths were pure.
an explanation of why dividing the octave into twelve identical semitones makes every interval sound more consonant.
the qualification of a triumphalist narrative by reframing an apparent improvement as a deliberate trade-off.
a chronological account of how successive tuning systems corrected one another's errors until the octave was divided accurately.
correct_answer: the qualification of a triumphalist narrative by reframing an apparent improvement as a deliberate trade-off.

passage: Critics have long praised Elizabeth Gaskell's industrial novels for their documentary fidelity, treating the factory scenes as near-transcriptions of conditions she had personally observed in Manchester. The assumption is flattering but misleading. The very features that read as unmediated reportage—the clipped Lancashire dialect, the unhurried catalogues of machinery—are, the manuscript evidence shows, the most heavily reworked passages in the novels, revised far more often than the melodramatic subplots that supposedly compromise her realism. What presents itself as fidelity to fact is therefore an achieved effect: a style laboriously constructed to efface the labor of its own construction. To call Gaskell a mere recorder of what she saw is thus to mistake her rarest technical accomplishment for an absence of technique. Her descriptive authority, the passage implies, derives less from the accident of having witnessed the mills than from her success in persuading readers that she had only reported, never composed.

choices: It presents a conventional critical judgment and then reinterprets the evidence behind that judgment to reach an opposing conclusion.

It traces the process by which a novelist gathered raw material for her industrial novels.
It compares two novelists' approaches to realism in order to determine which is more authentic.
correct_answer: It presents a conventional critical judgment and then reinterprets the evidence behind that judgment to reach an opposing conclusion.

passage:
Text 1: Conservation orthodoxy treats non-native species as a contagion: introduced organisms, freed from their coevolved predators, outcompete natives and collapse the diversity that took millennia to assemble. The imperative follows directly—identify the invader, and remove it. A species' provenance is, on this view, a reliable proxy for its ecological worth.

Text 2: The nativist framework mistakes origin for effect. Many introduced species integrate into food webs, pollinate crops, or stabilize soils that disturbance has stripped, while some natives, under altered conditions, turn destructive. What matters ecologically is a species' function in its present context, not the accident of where it evolved. To manage by provenance is to spend scarce effort uprooting harmless newcomers while ignoring the harm done by long-resident species.

choices: reliable only for those introduced species that arrive without their coevolved predators.

unreliable, because a species' geographic origin does not track its actual ecological impact.
correct_answer: unreliable, because a species' geographic origin does not track its actual ecological impact.

passage:
Text 1: Automation will not produce lasting unemployment. History reassures us: mechanized looms and tractors destroyed particular jobs, yet each wave of technology created new kinds of work that no one had foreseen. Displaced laborers were absorbed, over time, into occupations the old economy could not have named.

Text 2: The historical comfort assumes displaced workers can move into the new jobs. But past transitions swapped one kind of manual labor for another. If machines now master the cognitive tasks that once absorbed the displaced, the escape route those earlier workers took may be the very thing being closed.

passage: Critics often treat the unreliable narrator as fiction's great solvent of certainty, a device that dissolves any stable truth into competing perspectives. The device does the opposite. For a narrator to register as unreliable, the reader must detect the gap between what is said and what is the case—must, that is, reconstruct the very facts the narrator distorts. A story narrated by a liar is legible only because the reader triangulates toward a truth the liar conceals; unreliability is a technique for pointing at reality by the roundabout route of misdescribing it. Far from abandoning the notion of a determinate world, such fiction depends on the reader's confidence that one exists and can be inferred. The narrator who cannot be trusted thus presupposes a reader who trusts that trustworthiness is possible. What looks like radical skepticism is, on inspection, a covert affirmation of the standards it appears to flout.
prompt: The author would most likely agree with which statement?
choices: Unreliable narration shows that no determinate truth underlies a story, only a set of competing perspectives.
Readers cannot distinguish a reliable narrator from an unreliable one without evidence from outside the text.
Unreliable narration is a distinctively modern technique that earlier writers of fiction avoided.
Recognizing a narrator as unreliable depends on the reader's assumption that a determinate truth exists.
correct_answer: Recognizing a narrator as unreliable depends on the reader's assumption that a determinate truth exists.

The absence of a chart did not abolish power; it merely drove power underground, where it answered to no rule and could not be contested.

passage: Bilingual children are frequently said to enjoy a general "executive-function advantage"—better attention control and task-switching—attributed to the constant effort of managing two languages. Early studies reported such advantages, but a skeptic notes that these findings came disproportionately from small samples and were more likely to be published when the effect was positive. She hypothesizes that the reported advantage is inflated by this publication filter rather than reflecting a robust cognitive difference, and predicts a specific signature in the literature if she is right.

passage: Detective fiction is often praised as a celebration of reason—the triumph of a brilliant mind imposing clarity on chaos. This account captures the genre's surface while missing its deeper machinery. The classic whodunit does not primarily flatter the intellect; it soothes a social anxiety. A murder tears the fabric of a stable community; the detective's function is to localize the disruption in a single guilty individual, excise it, and restore the prior order as though the crime were an aberration rather than a symptom. The pleasure the form supplies is less the thrill of deduction than the reassurance that disorder is always someone's discrete fault and never the community's own condition. Its rationalism, in short, is in the service of its conservatism.

By tracing the whodunit's development from its earliest examples into its classic form
correct_answer: By conceding a conventional view of the genre before locating its appeal in a different, less obvious function

passage: When a cleaner wrasse, marked with a colored spot, scraped its body against surfaces after seeing itself in a mirror, some researchers hailed the fish as self-aware, extending to it a capacity long reserved for apes and dolphins. Caution is warranted. Passing the mark test may show only that an animal can associate a mirror reflection with its own body, a sensorimotor achievement that need not involve any concept of a self. The wrasse's ecology supplies a simpler reading: a fish whose living depends on detecting blemishes on other bodies might be primed to respond to a blemish wherever a reflection places it, with no inner spectator required. To infer rich self-awareness from the behavior is to assume that one impressive performance can be produced only by the most demanding mechanism—when a leaner one, well suited to the animal's way of life, will do.

correct_answer: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.

To recover the past is, unavoidably, to erase a different past.

passage: When a species vanishes from an ecosystem, we expect its role to vanish with it. The story of the American chestnut complicates that expectation. After blight erased the tree from eastern forests, oaks expanded to fill the gap, feeding the same deer and turkeys the chestnut once fed. Yet oaks produce nuts erratically, in boom-and-bust cycles the steady chestnut never had, so the animals now endure lean years the forest formerly spared them. A vacancy, it seems, can be filled without truly being replaced.

passage: The Impressionists are conventionally remembered as embattled radicals, spurned by the official Salon and painting in defiant poverty. There is truth in the image, but it flatters a more calculating reality. Excluded from the state-run Salon, painters like Monet and Degas did not merely suffer their exclusion; they turned to the emerging network of private dealers and independent exhibitions that was reshaping the art market. Dealers such as Paul Durand-Ruel cultivated collectors, staged solo shows, and stabilized prices—functions the Salon had never performed for living artists. The much-mythologized independent exhibitions were, among other things, shrewd commercial ventures that bypassed a gatekeeper the market was already rendering obsolete. To read Impressionism purely as aesthetic insurgency is to miss how neatly its rebellion aligned with, and profited from, a structural shift already underway in how art was sold.

single-handedly created the modern system of private art dealers
failed commercially because it alienated established collectors
correct_answer: coincided with and took advantage of changes already transforming the art market

passage:
Text 1

The doubling of English real wages after 1350 has a straightforward cause. The plague killed a third or more of the workforce, and with laborers suddenly scarce, survivors could command far higher pay. Wages rose because bodies were few and fields were many; the market did what markets do, translating scarcity into price.

Text 2

Scarcity alone cannot explain the gains. Parliament answered the labor shortage with the Statute of Labourers, freezing wages at pre-plague levels and criminalizing the movement of workers. That wages nonetheless climbed reveals not the frictionless operation of supply and demand but the failure of a determined effort to suppress it. The rise measures the limits of coercion as much as the arithmetic of scarcity; where lords enforced the statute effectively, wages stagnated for decades despite identical mortality.
prompt: Based on Text 2, how would its author most likely respond to the explanation offered in Text 1?
choices: By arguing that the plague had no meaningful effect on English wage levels.
By maintaining that the Statute of Labourers, backed by lords willing to enforce it, succeeded in holding wages at pre-plague levels across England.
By agreeing that scarcity pushed wages upward but adding that the actual outcome depended on whether legal efforts to restrain wages succeeded.
By concluding that market forces operate without friction once labor becomes scarce.
correct_answer: By agreeing that scarcity pushed wages upward but adding that the actual outcome depended on whether legal efforts to restrain wages succeeded.

passage:
Text 1
A representative's task is straightforward: to carry the expressed will of those who elected her into the assembly. When she substitutes her own judgment for their instructions, she ceases to represent them and begins to rule them. The ballot is a mandate, not a blank check; a legislator who votes against the clear preference of her district has, whatever her reasons, betrayed the office.

Text 2
To treat a representative as a mere conduit for constituents' momentary preferences is to misunderstand why we elect people rather than poll them. We choose a representative for her judgment, exercised on our behalf over matters most citizens have neither time nor information to weigh. She owes her constituents her diligence and her conscience—not her automatic compliance. A legislator who abandons her considered view the instant it diverges from the district's mood has surrendered the very faculty for which she was chosen.

choices: Whether a representative who votes against her district's clear preference has thereby failed in her duty.
Whether representatives ought to be selected through popular elections rather than by some other method of appointment.
Whether most citizens have the time and information needed to weigh every matter that comes before a legislature.
Whether a representative owes her constituents diligence in carrying out the office she holds.
correct_answer: Whether a representative who votes against her district's clear preference has thereby failed in her duty.

passage:
Text 1: The productivity of large cities is frequently credited to agglomeration—the idea that packing firms and workers together speeds the exchange of ideas. Denser labor markets let workers match to better-fitting jobs, and proximity lets knowledge "spill over" between firms. On this account, a city's output per worker rises mechanically with its size.

Text 2: Ling's longitudinal data trouble the standard story. When she tracked individual workers who moved from small towns to large cities, their wages did rise—but the gain appeared almost entirely at the moment of arrival, not through subsequent years of urban exposure. Workers did not become more productive by marinating in the city; rather, the most capable workers had selected into it. The city's apparent "spillover" was, in large part, a sorting effect that a snapshot of city-level averages cannot distinguish from genuine learning.

choices: By agreeing that large cities raise output per worker, but arguing the mechanism is faster job matching rather than knowledge spillover.
By conceding that knowledge spillovers exist but insisting they are too small to affect city-level averages.
By arguing that much of what looks like productivity gained within the city may instead reflect which workers chose to move there.
By denying that workers who move to large cities see any wage gains at all.
correct_answer: By arguing that much of what looks like productivity gained within the city may instead reflect which workers chose to move there.
